answers.q: How much electricity does one ChatGPT question use?

guess.prompt: One short ChatGPT question uses about as much electricity as…
options: A US home for a day

answers.reveal: One phone charge, about 19 Wh, is 10 to 80 short questions, depending on whose figure you use.
answers.answer: About 2% of a phone charge. OpenAI says an average question uses 0.34 Wh. Other published figures are 0.24 Wh (Google, for Gemini) and 1.86 Wh (one large open model, estimated by MIT Technology Review). They measure different things, so they can’t be ranked. Pasting in a long document can use about 7 to 120 times more (Epoch AI), and thinking modes about 30 times more on average (Hugging Face, open models).
answers.world: It adds up because there are so many: ChatGPT alone handled 18 billion messages a week by July 2025. At 0.34 Wh each, that’s about 0.32 TWh a year by Hum’s sums. All the world’s data centres together used about 485 TWh in 2025.

points.title: Published figures, measured different ways (not comparable)

items.label: One large open model, MIT Technology Review
items.how: one model, estimated by the magazine

dontknow: OpenAI hasn’t published how its 0.34 Wh is measured or what it includes.
No company publishes figures for its newest models or for long, document-heavy chats.
answers.share: One ChatGPT question uses about 2% of a phone charge (0.34 Wh, OpenAI’s figure). Billions of them add up: data centres used about 485 TWh in 2025.

answers.q: Does asking ChatGPT use 10 times more energy than a Google search?
answers.heard: “Asking ChatGPT uses 10 times the energy of a Google search.”
answers.reveal: The 10× compared an early estimate with a figure from 2009. On today’s figures they’re roughly level.
answers.answer: Out of date. The 10× came from the IEA’s 2024 report: 2.9 Wh for a ChatGPT request against 0.3 Wh for a Google search. The ChatGPT number traces back to an estimate of around 3 Wh by de Vries (2023), and the search number is Google’s own, from 2009. Newer figures for a short question are about ten times lower: Epoch AI estimates roughly 0.3 Wh and OpenAI says 0.34 Wh. So on today’s figures they’re roughly level, though nobody has published what a search uses now.
answers.world: All the world’s data centres, of which AI is one part, used about 485 TWh in 2025. That’s about as much electricity as France uses in a year, and around 1.5% of the world’s. The IEA expects it to roughly double by 2030.

dontknow: Google hasn’t published what a search uses today, with or without AI Overviews.
answers.share: “ChatGPT uses 10× a Google search” is out of date: newer figures put a short question at roughly 0.3 Wh, level with Google’s 2009 search figure.

answers.q: Does ChatGPT use a bottle of water for every email it writes?
answers.heard: “ChatGPT drinks a bottle of water for every email it writes.”
answers.result: Not for the model that was measured. For today’s, nobody has published it
answers.reveal: The peer-reviewed study said one 500 ml bottle per 10 to 50 answers, for GPT-3.
answers.answer: Nobody has published it for today’s models. The best-known study (Li et al., UC Riverside) estimated GPT-3 used a 500 ml bottle for every 10 to 50 medium-length answers: 10 to 50 ml each. Company figures are far lower: OpenAI says about 0.32 ml per average question and Google 0.26 ml per median prompt, and neither says clearly whether it counts water used at power plants. A newer figure for an AI-written email also circulates, but Hum couldn’t read it on its page, so it isn’t used.
answers.world: Water is felt locally. In a recent year, US data centres used about 17 billion gallons on site, and about 211 billion more through the power plants that supplied them (Berkeley Lab estimates).

answers.q: Is asking ChatGPT worse than streaming Netflix?
answers.heard: “One ChatGPT question uses more energy than an hour of Netflix.”
answers.heardFrom: a common worry in comment threads
answers.result: No: an hour of streaming is about 41 to 230 questions
answers.reveal: An hour of Netflix, about 77 Wh in 2019 by the IEA’s estimate, is about 230 short questions at OpenAI’s figure.
answers.answer: No. The IEA estimated an hour of Netflix in 2019 used about 77 Wh across data centres, networks and your screen. That’s about 230 short questions at OpenAI’s 0.34 Wh, and about 41 even at the highest published figure (1.86 Wh). It’s a rough comparison: the streaming figure is from 2019 and includes your device, while the question figures cover only the data centre.
answers.world: All the world’s data centres, of which AI is one part, used about 485 TWh in 2025. That’s about as much electricity as France uses in a year, and around 1.5% of the world’s. The IEA expects it to roughly double by 2030.
answers.why: It compares one question with an hour of video, and the two figures count different things.
dontknow: The IEA hasn’t updated its streaming figure since 2019.
answers.share: An hour of Netflix used about as much electricity as 41 to 230 short ChatGPT questions (IEA, 2019; OpenAI and MIT Technology Review figures).

answers.q: Is using AI worse for the climate than taking a flight?
answers.heard: “Using AI is as bad for the climate as flying.”
answers.reveal: One 1,000 km domestic flight is roughly a million short questions.
answers.answer: No, for ordinary chatting. A 1,000 km domestic flight emits about 246 kg of CO₂e per passenger by UK government factors (via Our World in Data), which include the extra warming of emissions at altitude. A short question at OpenAI’s 0.34 Wh on the world-average grid is about 0.16 g of CO₂. So the flight equals about 1.5 million questions, or about 0.8 million counting the flight’s CO₂ alone. Even at the highest published figure on a coal-heavy grid, about 1.04 g a question, it’s over 100,000. AI video and all-day coding agents use far more per task.
answers.world: All the world’s data centres, of which AI is one part, used about 485 TWh in 2025. That’s about as much electricity as France uses in a year, and around 1.5% of the world’s. The IEA expects it to roughly double by 2030.
answers.why: It sets one person’s chatting against one person’s flight. The comparison that matters is the total.
dontknow: There’s no solid public figure for heavy uses like coding agents running all day.
answers.share: One 1,000 km domestic flight is about 0.8 to 1.5 million short AI questions in CO₂ (UK factors via Our World in Data; OpenAI’s 0.34 Wh; world-average grid).

answers.q: Do “thinking” modes use more energy than normal answers?
answers.heard: “Thinking modes use far more energy than a normal answer.”
answers.reveal: Measured on open models: about 30 times more on average.
answers.answer: Yes. Hugging Face’s AI Energy Score team measured open models directly. Reasoning models used about 30 times more energy on average than models without reasoning, and the same model used 150 to 700 times more with reasoning switched on. Most of the difference is length: the hidden “thinking” is extra text the model writes. These are open models, not ChatGPT, whose company hasn’t published figures for its thinking modes.
answers.world: One person’s share is small, but the total keeps growing: electricity use by AI-focused data centres grew 50% in 2025, by the IEA’s estimate.
dontknow: OpenAI, Google and Anthropic don’t publish energy per answer for their thinking modes.
answers.share: Thinking modes use far more energy: about 30× more on average in Hugging Face’s measurements of open models, and 150 to 700× for the same model with reasoning on.

answers.q: How much does my ChatGPT use add to my carbon footprint in a year?

guess.prompt: A typical ChatGPT user’s year of questions makes about…

answers.result: About 0.2 kg of CO₂ a year
answers.reveal: About 26 questions a week at 0.34 Wh each, on the world-average grid.
answers.answer: About 0.2 kg of CO₂ a year, by Hum’s sums. OpenAI’s own usage paper reports 18 billion messages a week from 700 million users, about 26 each a week. At 0.34 Wh each, that’s about 0.46 kWh a year, or about 0.2 kg on the world-average grid. Even 50 questions a day comes to about 3 kg. An average person’s fossil CO₂ is about 4.8 tonnes a year. This counts answering questions only, not training models, making chips or building data centres.
answers.world: One person’s share is small, but the total keeps growing: electricity use by AI-focused data centres grew 50% in 2025, by the IEA’s estimate.
dontknow: Use is very uneven, and OpenAI gives only an average.
The grids behind ChatGPT’s data centres aren’t published, so the world average stands in.
Training, chips and buildings aren’t counted here.
answers.share: A typical ChatGPT user’s year of questions: about 0.2 kg of CO₂ (Hum’s sums from OpenAI’s figures). The build-out behind it is growing fast: AI data centres used 50% more electricity in 2025.

answers.q: Are big tech companies’ emissions going up because of AI?
answers.heard: “Big tech’s emissions are rising because of AI.”
answers.heardFrom: news coverage of the companies’ reports
answers.result: Rising, yes. How much is AI, they don’t say
answers.reveal: Google’s footprint rose 18% in 2025, and Microsoft’s emissions 25% in its 2025 fiscal year, by their own reports.
answers.answer: Their emissions are rising, by their own 2026 reports as covered by trade press. Google’s 2025 carbon footprint rose 18% on the year before while its electricity use grew 37%. Microsoft’s emissions rose 25% in its 2025 fiscal year, to 20.29 million tonnes of CO₂e. Google says its electricity-related (scope 2) emissions fell 3%. Neither company says how much of the rise is AI rather than its other data-centre work.
answers.world: All the world’s data centres, of which AI is one part, used about 485 TWh in 2025. That’s about as much electricity as France uses in a year, and around 1.5% of the world’s. The IEA expects it to roughly double by 2030.
answers.why: That emissions are rising is true. That AI is the cause is the part the companies don’t break out.
dontknow: Neither company separates AI from its other data-centre work.
Hum read these figures in trade-press reports; the company reports themselves still need checking on the page.
answers.share: By their own reports: Google’s footprint rose 18% in 2025 (electricity use up 37%), Microsoft’s emissions 25% in fiscal 2025. How much is AI, they don’t say.

answers.q: Are data centres making my electricity bill go up?
answers.heard: “Data centres are pushing up everyone’s electricity bills.”
answers.result: Partly: in the eastern US, the grid’s monitor says yes
answers.reveal: In the PJM grid of the eastern US, the independent market monitor calls data centres the primary reason capacity prices jumped.
answers.answer: Partly, depending on where you live. In the eastern US grid run by PJM, the independent market monitor calls data-centre growth the primary reason capacity prices jumped. By its estimate of what prices would have been without them, data-centre load raised one capacity auction’s revenue by $7.3 billion (82%), and makes up about 9% of the wholesale price of power. These are the monitor’s estimates, not measured bills: what reaches your bill depends on your utility and state.
answers.world: Outside PJM, Hum has no checked figure yet for how data centres affect household bills.
answers.why: True in some regions, stated as if it were true everywhere.
dontknow: Nobody has measured how much of a given household’s bill increase is caused by data centres.
Hum read these figures in Utility Dive’s reporting; the monitor’s own reports still need checking on the page.
Hum hasn’t yet sourced other estimates, from utilities, industry or researchers.
answers.share: In the eastern US PJM grid, the independent market monitor estimates data-centre load raised one capacity auction’s revenue by $7.3 billion (82%). What reaches your bill depends on your utility.

answers.q: Are data centres powered by coal, gas or renewables?

guess.prompt: Which source supplies the most electricity to the world’s data centres today?

answers.result: Mostly fossil fuels: coal about 30%, gas 26%
answers.reveal: Coal is the largest single source at about 30%, then renewables at 27%, gas at 26% and nuclear at 15%.
answers.answer: Mostly fossil fuels. By the IEA’s estimate (Energy and AI, 2025), the electricity data centres use worldwide comes about 30% from coal, 26% from gas, 27% from renewables (mainly wind, solar and hydro) and 15% from nuclear. It’s shaped by where data centres are: the US used 45% of the total and China 25%. That’s the grid they draw from, not what companies buy on paper, which is why “fully renewable” claims can differ.
answers.world: Looking ahead, the IEA expects renewables to meet about half of the growth in data-centre demand.
dontknow: The IEA page doesn’t give the exact year for this split.
No industry-wide figure exists for renewables bought through contracts.
answers.share: The world’s data centres run mostly on fossil fuels: about 30% coal and 26% gas, with 27% renewables and 15% nuclear (IEA, Energy and AI 2025).

answers.q: What share of the world’s electricity do data centres use?

guess.prompt: What share of the world’s electricity did data centres use in 2024?

answers.reveal: About 415 TWh in 2024, and 485 TWh in 2025: about as much as France uses in a year.
answers.answer: About 1.5% of the world’s electricity in 2024, or 415 TWh, by the IEA’s estimate. It grew to about 485 TWh in 2025, about as much as France uses in a year. AI is one part: in the US, AI servers used about 26.5% to 38% of data-centre electricity. Use is concentrated: the US used 45% of the world total, China 25% and Europe 15%. So in a few places, like Ireland or Northern Virginia, data centres are a much bigger share of local demand.
answers.world: The IEA expects data centres to use about 950 TWh by 2030, roughly double 2025.
dontknow: Nobody keeps an official count of the world’s data centres.
There’s no world figure for AI’s share; the US one stands in.
answers.share: Data centres used about 1.5% of the world’s electricity in 2024 (IEA). By 2025 that was about as much as France uses in a year, and the IEA expects it to roughly double by 2030.
